article-3.x: A felony is an act or omission punished by the Revised Penal Code. It can be committed in two ways. By dolo (deceit), the offender acts on purpose with criminal intent. By culpa (fault), harm results from imprudence, negligence, lack of foresight or lack of skill.
k: Elements of a felony: (1) an act or omission; (2) punishable by the RPC; (3) done by means of dolo or culpa.
Dolo requires freedom, intelligence and intent.
Culpa requires freedom, intelligence, and imprudence, negligence, lack of skill or lack of foresight.
Actus non facit reum nisi mens sit rea: the act is not criminal unless the mind is criminal (for felonies).
article-3.w: It ties criminal liability to a blameworthy state of mind, so accidents and good-faith acts are not punished as crimes.
t: Mala in se (RPC felonies: intent matters) versus mala prohibita (special laws: the act itself is punished, and good faith is generally no defense).
Reckless imprudence is a crime in itself under Art. 365, not just a mode of committing another felony (Ivler v. Modesto-San Pedro).
Motive is different from intent. Motive is generally immaterial, except to identify the accused or when the evidence is circumstantial.
q: What are the requisites of dolo? Of culpa?
Is good faith a defense in mala prohibita?

article-4.x: You are criminally liable (1) for the wrong you actually cause while committing a felony, even if it differs from what you intended, and (2) for an impossible crime — when you try to commit a crime against persons or property, but it cannot happen because it is inherently impossible or because the means you used were inadequate or ineffectual.
k: Par. 1 (praeter intentionem, error in personae, aberratio ictus): the offender must be committing a felony, and the wrong done must be the direct, natural and logical consequence of it (proximate cause).

Par. 2 (impossible crime): the act would be a crime against persons or property; it was done with evil intent; its accomplishment is inherently impossible or the means are inadequate or ineffectual; and the act is not punished by another provision.
The penalty for an impossible crime is in Art. 59.
article-4.w: Par. 1 makes wrongdoers answer for the consequences of their crimes. Par. 2 punishes criminal tendency even when no harm results.
t: The felony must be the proximate cause — an efficient intervening cause breaks the chain.
Impossible crime applies only to crimes against persons or property. Factual impossibility counts (Intod v. CA).
Under par. 1 the offender must be committing a felony, not merely a lawful act.
q: Distinguish error in personae, aberratio ictus and praeter intentionem.
Give the elements of an impossible crime.

d.h: The accused fired at the bedroom where they believed the victim slept, but she was not home. This was an impossible crime: factual impossibility, where an extraneous circumstance unknown to the actor prevents the crime, falls under Art. 4(2).
d.r: Factual impossibility is covered by Art. 4(2).

article-6.x: A felony is punished whether consummated, frustrated or attempted. It is consummated when all its elements are present. It is frustrated when the offender has done every act needed to produce the felony, but it does not happen for reasons independent of his will. It is attempted when he begins by overt acts but does not complete all of them, for reasons other than his own spontaneous desistance.
k: Attempted: overt acts commenced; not all acts of execution performed; non-completion due to causes other than spontaneous desistance.
Frustrated: all acts of execution performed; felony not produced; by causes independent of the offender’s will.
Consummated: all elements present.
Subjective phase (offender still controls) versus objective phase (beyond his control).
article-6.w: It grades liability by how close the offender came to completing the crime.
t: Some crimes have no frustrated stage, e.g., rape (People v. Orita) and theft (Valenzuela v. People).
Spontaneous desistance during the attempted stage exempts from liability for the attempted felony, but not for any other crime already committed.
In homicide or murder, a frustrated stage requires a mortal wound that would have caused death without timely medical help.
q: Why is there no frustrated theft?
What is the effect of spontaneous desistance?

d.h: Rape has no frustrated stage. Entry of the labia, however slight, consummates it; without it, the crime is only attempted.
Theft is consummated once the offender gains possession of the thing, even if he has no opportunity to dispose of it. Theft therefore cannot be frustrated.

article-8.x: Conspiracy and proposal to commit a felony are punished only when the law specially provides for it. There is conspiracy when two or more persons agree to commit a felony and decide to commit it. There is proposal when a person who has decided to commit a felony proposes its execution to others.
k: Conspiracy as a crime: punished only in specific cases (e.g., treason, rebellion, coup d’état, sedition).
Conspiracy as a mode of committing a crime: once proved, the act of one is the act of all.
It may be inferred from conduct before, during and after the crime showing a joint purpose and community of interest.
article-8.w: Group criminality is more dangerous, so the law treats all conspirators as equally liable once they act on the agreement.
t: Mere presence at the scene, or knowledge of the plan without participation, is not conspiracy.
A conspirator who desists before the crime is committed may escape liability for the crime itself.
q: Distinguish conspiracy as a crime from conspiracy as a manner of incurring liability.

article-11.x: These are justifying circumstances. The person who acts under them commits no crime at all and has no civil liability (except under par. 4, state of necessity, where those benefited pay). The act is treated as lawful.
k: Self-defense: (1) unlawful aggression; (2) reasonable necessity of the means employed to prevent or repel it; (3) lack of sufficient provocation on the part of the person defending himself.
Defense of relatives and of strangers carry modified third requisites.
State of necessity: the evil sought to be avoided actually exists; the injury feared is greater than that done; and there is no other practical and less harmful means.
Fulfillment of duty; obedience to a lawful order of a superior.
article-11.w: The law does not demand that people submit to unlawful attack, and it does not punish acts it actually permits or commands.
t: Unlawful aggression is indispensable. Without it there is no self-defense, complete or incomplete.
Aggression must be actual or imminent; it ceases when the aggressor retreats or is disarmed.
Pleading self-defense admits the killing; the burden shifts to the accused to prove it by clear and convincing evidence.
Reasonable necessity is judged by the circumstances as they appeared to the defender, not by mathematical equality of weapons.
q: What is the indispensable requisite of self-defense?
Who bears civil liability in a state of necessity?

article-12.x: These are exempting circumstances. The act is wrongful, but the person is not criminally liable because one of the conditions of voluntariness — intelligence, freedom or intent — is missing. Civil liability generally remains.
k: Imbecile or insane person (unless acting in a lucid interval).
Minors: under RA 9344 (as amended by RA 10630), a child 15 or below is exempt; above 15 but below 18 is exempt unless he acted with discernment.
Accident without fault or intention while doing a lawful act with due care.
Compulsion of irresistible force; uncontrollable fear of an equal or greater injury.
Failure to perform an act required by law, when prevented by a lawful or insuperable cause.
article-12.w: Punishment presupposes a free and intelligent choice; where it is absent, the person is not blameworthy.
t: Paragraphs 2 and 3 on age have been superseded by RA 9344 — always cite the current ages.
Insanity must exist at the time of the act and must be a complete deprivation of intelligence or freedom of will; it is proved by clear and convincing evidence.
Exempting circumstances leave civil liability (Art. 101); justifying circumstances generally do not.
q: What ages are exempt under RA 9344?
Distinguish justifying from exempting circumstances as to civil liability.

article-13.x: Mitigating circumstances lower the penalty. They do not erase guilt. They show reduced blameworthiness: youth, lack of intent to commit so grave a wrong, provocation, passion, voluntary surrender, plea of guilty, physical defects, illness, and similar circumstances.
k: Ordinary mitigating circumstances may be offset by aggravating ones (Art. 64).
Privileged mitigating circumstances (e.g., minority, incomplete justification or exemption under Art. 69) lower the penalty by one or two degrees and cannot be offset.
Voluntary surrender: not actually arrested; surrender to a person in authority or his agent; spontaneous.
Plea of guilty: spontaneous, in open court, before the prosecution presents evidence.
t: Passion or obfuscation and vindication of a grave offense cannot be appreciated together if they arise from the same facts.
The catch-all paragraph 10 allows any circumstance of similar nature and analogous to those listed.
q: What are the requisites of voluntary surrender?
How do privileged mitigating circumstances differ from ordinary ones?

article-14.x: Aggravating circumstances raise the penalty because they show greater perversity, greater danger, or an aggravated injury. Examples are treachery, evident premeditation, abuse of superior strength, nighttime, dwelling, recidivism, and cruelty.
k: Generic (can be offset by mitigating circumstances), specific, qualifying (change the nature of the crime — e.g., treachery turns homicide into murder), and inherent.
Treachery (alevosia): means of execution that ensure the crime without risk to the offender from the defense the victim might make, deliberately adopted.
Evident premeditation: time the offender decided to commit the crime; an overt act showing he clung to it; and enough time to reflect.
Under the Rules of Criminal Procedure, qualifying and aggravating circumstances must be alleged in the information to be appreciated.
article-14.w: The law punishes more severely those who commit crimes in ways that show greater malice or that exploit the victim’s helplessness.
t: Treachery must be present at the inception of the attack.
Recidivism (a previous conviction by final judgment for a crime in the same title) is distinct from reiteracion, habitual delinquency and quasi-recidivism.
Aggravating circumstances not alleged in the information cannot be considered, even if proved.
q: What are the elements of treachery?
Distinguish recidivism, reiteracion, habitual delinquency and quasi-recidivism.

article-48.x: When a single act constitutes two or more grave or less grave felonies (compound crime), or when one offense is a necessary means for committing the other (complex crime proper), only one penalty is imposed: the penalty for the most serious crime, applied in its maximum period.
k: Compound crime: a single act results in two or more grave or less grave felonies.
Complex crime proper: one offense is the necessary means to commit the other.
The penalty is that for the most serious crime, in its maximum period.
article-48.w: A single criminal impulse is treated as a single crime, but punished more heavily.
t: Light felonies are not complexed.
Special complex crimes (e.g., robbery with homicide, rape with homicide) are fixed by law and are not governed by Art. 48.
Art. 48 cannot be applied if it would impose a heavier penalty than separate prosecution.
q: Distinguish compound crimes from complex crimes proper.
Why is robbery with homicide not an Art. 48 complex crime?

article-266-a.x: Rape is committed in two ways. First, by a man who has carnal knowledge of a woman through force, threat or intimidation; when she is deprived of reason or unconscious; by fraudulent machination or grave abuse of authority; or when she is below the statutory age, even without those circumstances. Second, by sexual assault: inserting the penis into another person’s mouth or anal orifice, or any instrument or object into the genital or anal orifice of another, under the same circumstances.
k: Rape by sexual intercourse: offender is a man; carnal knowledge of a woman; under the circumstances listed.
Rape by sexual assault: any person; the insertion described; under the same circumstances.
Statutory rape: the victim is below the statutory age. RA 11648 (2022) raised the age to below 16, with a close-in-age exemption under the conditions stated there.
RA 8353 reclassified rape as a crime against persons (no longer a private crime).
article-266-a.w: It protects bodily integrity and sexual autonomy. For statutory rape, the law conclusively treats a child as incapable of consent.
t: Use the age as amended by RA 11648, not the original “under twelve.”
In statutory rape, force and consent are immaterial; proof of age and of the act suffices.
There is no frustrated rape (People v. Orita).
q: What is the current age for statutory rape?
Distinguish the two modes of committing rape.
